Rationale: MC narrows the back-calculation clause to 'in isotope dilution procedures'. That is one use case among several — the mass is equally needed for straight concentration work. Q/SF is the more general statement and already covers ID. Nothing is lost.
Adopted description: Mass (mg) of solid material digested or volume (mL) of liquid taken for dissolution. Used for yield calculations and concentration back-calculation.

MC (Solution MC v4): Mass (mg) of solid material digested or volume (mL) of liquid taken for dissolution. Used for yield calculations and concentration back-calculation in isotope dilution procedures.

Rationale: Both variants are identical except for the worked example, and the two examples give the two canonical reasons a second step is needed: refractory residue (Q/SF) and fluoride-complex destruction (MC). Neither subsumes the other, so both are kept.
Adopted description: Total number of distinct acid digestion steps required to dissolve the sample. Some procedures require multiple sequential steps — for example, an initial open-beaker HF–HNO3 dissolution followed by a second closed-vessel step for residues retaining refractory minerals, or by an aqua regia reflux to destroy fluoride complexes.
Q (Solution Q v6): Total number of distinct acid digestion steps required to dissolve the sample. Some procedures require multiple sequential steps (e.g., an initial open-beaker HF–HNO3 dissolution followed by a second closed-vessel step for residues retaining refractory minerals).
SF (Solution SF v6): Total number of distinct acid digestion steps required to dissolve the sample. Some procedures require multiple sequential steps (e.g., an initial open-beaker HF–HNO3 dissolution followed by a second closed-vessel step for residues retaining refractory minerals).
MC (Solution MC v4): Total number of distinct acid digestion steps required to dissolve the sample. Some procedures require multiple sequential steps (e.g., open-beaker HF–HNO3 dissolution followed by aqua regia reflux to destroy fluoride complexes).

Rationale: SF and MC add a concrete consequence — which vessel class is required for complete silicate digestion — that tells the user how to choose. Q states only that vessel type matters, without saying what follows from it.

Rationale: MC is a strict superset of SF and adds real consequence content: incomplete dissolution fractionates isotopes. The clause is conditional ('for isotope ratio work'), naming a purpose rather than an analyser, so it generalises to any consumer doing that work.
Adopted description: Acid mixture used for sample dissolution. Record acid type(s) and concentration(s) where known (e.g., concentrated HF–HNO3 in Parr bombs is standard for silicate dissolution). For isotope-ratio work, complete matrix dissolution is required to avoid isotopic fractionation during partial dissolution.
Q (Solution Q v6): Acid mixture used for sample dissolution. Record acid type(s) and concentration(s) where known (e.g., concentrated HF–HNO3, HNO3–HCl).
SF (Solution SF v6): Acid mixture used for sample dissolution. Record acid type(s) and concentration(s) where known (e.g., concentrated HF–HNO3 in Parr bombs is standard for silicate dissolution).
MC (Solution MC v4): Acid mixture used for sample dissolution. Record acid type(s) and concentration(s) where known (e.g., concentrated HF–HNO3 in Parr bombs is standard for silicate dissolution). For isotope ratio work, complete matrix dissolution is required to avoid isotopic fractionation during partial dissolution.

Rationale: MC has by far the best reasoning — it says WHY separation is needed (variable mass bias, isobaric interference) where Q/SF only say it is common. But MC names the analyser twice ('prior to MC-ICP-MS analysis', 'mandatory for solution MC-ICP-MS'), which disqualifies it as module text. Adopted here is SF's general frame carrying MC's reasoning, with the analyser references converted to the purpose they actually denote. This is the row where a separation chemist may disagree with the phrasing 'usually mandatory for isotope-ratio procedures'.
Adopted description: Whether chromatographic separation of element groups (e.g., using ion exchange resin) was performed prior to analysis. Separation may be required to remove matrix elements that cause variable mass bias, to eliminate isobaric interferences, or to isolate an element group before measurement (e.g., Fe and Cu–Zn for isotope dilution, Hf separation from REE, removal of Cr and Ni from Fe fractions). It is usually mandatory for isotope-ratio procedures and optional for concentration measurement. Record resin type and elution matrix conditions if applied. Record 'None' if the direct digestion solution is analyzed.
Q (Solution Q v6): Whether chromatographic separation of element groups (e.g., using ion exchange resin) was performed prior to ICP-MS analysis. Common for procedures requiring matrix removal or interference elimination before measurement (e.g., Fe and Cu–Zn for isotope dilution). Record resin type and matrix conditions if applied. Record 'None' if direct digestion solution is analyzed.
SF (Solution SF v6): Whether chromatographic separation of element groups (e.g., using ion exchange resin) was performed prior to ICP-MS analysis. Common for procedures requiring matrix removal or interference elimination before measurement (e.g., Fe and Cu–Zn for isotope dilution, Hf separation from REE). Record resin type and matrix conditions if applied. Record 'None' if direct digestion solution is analyzed.
MC (Solution MC v4): Whether chromatographic separation was performed prior to MC-ICP-MS analysis. Separation is usually mandatory for solution MC-ICP-MS to remove matrix elements that cause variable mass bias and to eliminate isobaric interferences (e.g., removal of Cr and Ni from Fe fractions; separation of U from matrix). Record resin type and elution matrix. Record 'None' if direct digestion solution is analyzed (uncommon for isotope ratio work).

Rationale: MC adds when the spike must be introduced and why — genuine instruction content the other two lack.
Adopted description: Isotopic spike material added to the sample before or during digestion for isotope dilution (ID) analysis or double-spike mass bias correction. For double-spike procedures, the spike must be added and equilibrated before digestion to correct for any isotopic fractionation during dissolution and column chemistry. For concentration ID, the spike must be added before digestion for complete equilibration. Record spike name or certificate reference, spike isotopes, and whether added pre- or post-digestion. Record 'None' if ID or double-spike technique is not used.
Q (Solution Q v6): Isotopic spike material added to the sample before or during digestion for isotope dilution (ID) analysis. Record spike name or certificate reference and spike isotope(s). Record 'None' if ID technique is not used.
SF (Solution SF v6): Isotopic spike material added to the sample before or during digestion for isotope dilution (ID) analysis. Spike must be added before digestion for complete equilibration. Record spike name or certificate reference and spike isotope(s). Record 'None' if ID technique is not used.
MC (Solution MC v4): Isotopic spike material added to the sample before or during digestion for isotope dilution (ID) analysis or double-spike mass bias correction. For double-spike procedures, the spike must be added and equilibrated before digestion to correct for any isotopic fractionation during dissolution and column chemistry. For concentration ID, the spike must be added before digestion for complete equilibration. Record spike name or certificate reference, spike isotopes, and whether added pre- or post-digestion. Record 'None' if ID or double-spike technique is not used.

Rationale: MC contributes the strongest consequence in the whole module — molarity must be matched between samples and bracketing standards or mass bias shifts. SF contributes a second real fact, that trace HF may be added to keep HFSE in solution, but wraps it in 'some SF-ICP-MS procedures', which names an analyser. Both facts are kept, both generalised.
Adopted description: Acid type and concentration of the final dissolved sample solution introduced to the instrument. Directly affects instrument response and ion transmission. For isotope-ratio procedures, acid molarity must be precisely matched between samples and bracketing standards to avoid matrix-induced mass bias offsets. Procedures targeting HFSE may add trace HF to the final solution to keep those elements in solution.
Q (Solution Q v6): Acid type and concentration of the final dissolved sample solution introduced to the instrument. Directly affects instrument response and ion transmission.
SF (Solution SF v6): Acid type and concentration of the final dissolved sample solution introduced to the instrument. Directly affects instrument response and ion transmission. Note: some SF-ICP-MS procedures add trace HF to final solution to stabilize HFSE.
MC (Solution MC v4): Acid type and concentration of the final dissolved sample solution introduced to the instrument. Critical for isotope ratio work: acid molarity must be precisely matched between samples and bracketing standards to avoid matrix-induced mass bias offsets.

Rationale: This is the one case where the majority variant is the worse one. SF and MC say the nebulizer 'affects droplet size distribution and uptake rate' — but `Sample Uptake Rate` is a separate field in this same module, so that wording blurs the boundary between two adjacent fields. Q's 'sample introduction efficiency' names the property the nebulizer actually governs and keeps the two distinct. 2-of-3 agreement is not evidence here.
Adopted description: Type and material of the pneumatic nebulizer used for sample introduction. Affects droplet size distribution and sample introduction efficiency.
Q (Solution Q v6): Type and material of the pneumatic nebulizer used for sample introduction. Affects droplet size distribution and sample introduction efficiency.
SF (Solution SF v6): Type and material of the pneumatic nebulizer used for sample introduction. Affects droplet size distribution and uptake rate.
MC (Solution MC v4): Type and material of the pneumatic nebulizer used for sample introduction. Affects droplet size distribution and uptake rate.

Field: Spray Chamber Type and Cooling Temperature
Rationale: MC adds two clauses. The second is genuine boundary content — it explains that a spray chamber may sit downstream of a desolvating nebulizer, which is how this field relates to `Desolvation System`. The first ('Scott double-pass and cyclonic are standard') merely restates Column F and is dropped, per 6.4.
Adopted description: Type of spray chamber and cooling temperature if thermostatted (°C). Chamber type and temperature control aerosol droplet size and the solvent vapor load reaching the plasma. In some procedures a spray chamber is placed downstream of a desolvating nebulizer to improve signal stability.
Q (Solution Q v6): Type of spray chamber and cooling temperature if thermostatted (°C). Chamber type and temperature control aerosol droplet size and the solvent vapor load reaching the plasma.
SF (Solution SF v6): Type of spray chamber and cooling temperature if thermostatted (°C). Chamber type and temperature control aerosol droplet size and the solvent vapor load reaching the plasma.
MC (Solution MC v4): Type of spray chamber and cooling temperature if thermostatted (°C). Chamber type and temperature control aerosol droplet size and solvent vapor load reaching the plasma. Scott double-pass and cyclonic chambers are standard; in some procedures a spray chamber is placed downstream of a desolvating nebulizer to improve signal stability.

Rationale: MC alone states the TRADE-OFF — desolvation buys sensitivity but costs mass bias stability — which is the most valuable kind of consequence content because it tells the user when not to use it. Its 'Frequently used in MC-ICP-MS' wrapper is removed. Q's ApexQ and SF's Aridus-I product examples are dropped from the description; Column F already lists both.
Adopted description: Desolvating nebulizer or membrane desolvator used upstream of the plasma to reduce solvent load. Lowers oxide production rates and increases sensitivity, and is commonly used for low-abundance analytes or small sample sizes. Note the trade-off: desolvation can introduce additional instrumental mass bias instability relative to wet plasma introduction. Record 'None' if not used.
Q (Solution Q v6): Desolvating nebulizer or membrane desolvator used upstream of the plasma to reduce solvent load. Lowers oxide production rates and increases sensitivity for selected element groups (e.g., ApexQ for chalcophile elements). Record 'None' if not used.
SF (Solution SF v6): Desolvating nebulizer or membrane desolvator used upstream of the plasma to reduce solvent load. Reduces oxide production rates and increases sensitivity for selected element groups. Specific systems (e.g., Aridus-I) are often assigned to particular element fractions in multi-fraction procedures. Record 'None' if not used.
MC (Solution MC v4): Desolvating nebulizer or membrane desolvator used upstream of the plasma to reduce solvent load, increase sensitivity, and lower oxide production rates. Frequently used in MC-ICP-MS for low-abundance isotopes or small sample sizes. Note that desolvation can introduce additional instrumental mass bias instability compared to wet introduction systems. Record 'None' if not used.

Adopted description: Peristaltic pump speed or self-aspiration flow rate for sample introduction (µL/min or mL/min).
Q (Solution Q v6): Peristaltic pump speed or self-aspiration flow rate for sample introduction (µL/min or mL/min).
SF (Solution SF v6): Peristaltic pump speed or self-aspiration flow rate for sample introduction (µL/min or mL/min).
MC (Solution MC v4): Peristaltic pump speed or self-aspiration flow rate for sample introduction (µL/min or mL/min).

Rationale: MC adds 'and stability. Adjusted daily to optimize signal.' That is instruction content, and it is also the justification for the field's D=Editable tier — it tells the analyst this is a session-tuned parameter rather than a fixed procedure commitment.
Adopted description: Flow rate of the carrier argon gas delivered through the nebulizer (L/min). Controls aerosol transport and strongly influences signal sensitivity and stability. Adjusted daily to optimize signal.
Q (Solution Q v6): Flow rate of the carrier argon gas delivered through the nebulizer (L/min). Controls aerosol transport and strongly influences signal sensitivity.
SF (Solution SF v6): Flow rate of the carrier argon gas delivered through the nebulizer (L/min). Controls aerosol transport and strongly influences signal sensitivity.
MC (Solution MC v4): Flow rate of the carrier argon gas delivered through the nebulizer (L/min). Controls aerosol transport and strongly influences signal sensitivity and stability. Adjusted daily to optimize signal.

Rationale: MC adds a conditional consequence — incomplete washout cross-contaminates samples of differing isotopic composition — that names a purpose, not an analyser, and is equally true of isotope dilution work on a quadrupole.
Adopted description: Duration of instrument rinse between successive sample solutions (seconds). Controls carryover and memory effects. For isotope-ratio work, complete washout is critical to prevent cross-contamination between samples with differing isotopic compositions.
Q (Solution Q v6): Duration of instrument rinse between successive sample solutions (seconds). Controls carryover and memory effects.
SF (Solution SF v6): Duration of instrument rinse between successive sample solutions (seconds). Controls carryover and memory effects.
MC (Solution MC v4): Duration of instrument rinse between successive sample solutions (seconds). Controls carryover and memory effects. For isotope ratio work, complete washout is critical to prevent cross-contamination between samples with differing isotopic compositions.
